title: From Plessy to Brown
short: Plessy v. Ferguson (1896) upheld "separate but equal"; the NAACP's cases (Missouri ex rel. Gaines, 1938; Sweatt v. Painter, 1950) found separate graduate schools unequal; Brown v. Board of Education (1954), unanimous, held separate schools "inherently unequal," and Brown II (1955) ordered desegregation "with all deliberate speed."
trouble: Students think Brown overruled Plessy everywhere at once. Brown addressed public education; later per curiam orders applied it to beaches, buses, parks and other public facilities.

blocks.html: Note: This is an educational course, not legal advice.
The path from "separate but equal" to Brown is the most studied campaign in American law. It shows how equal protection was narrowed, then rebuilt case by case.

opts.facts: Louisiana's Separate Car Act of 1890 required railroads to provide "equal but separate" cars for white and Black passengers. Homer Plessy, who was one-eighth African in ancestry, sat in a car for white passengers as a planned test of the law and was arrested.
opts.reasoning: Justice Brown wrote that the amendment secured legal equality, not social equality, and that separation did not stamp one race as inferior unless people chose to read it that way.
opts.dissent: Justice Harlan, the only dissenter, wrote: "Our Constitution is color-blind, and neither knows nor tolerates classes among citizens," and predicted the decision would prove as harmful as Dred Scott.

blocks.html: The NAACP's lawyers, led by Charles Hamilton Houston and then Thurgood Marshall, did not attack Plessy head on at first. They held states to the "equal" half of the rule in graduate schools, where inequality was easiest to prove. Missouri ex rel. Gaines v. Canada (1938): Missouri could not send Black law students out of state. Sweatt v. Painter (1950): a hastily created Black law school in Texas was not equal to the University of Texas in faculty, library, reputation or the chance to meet future colleagues. McLaurin v. Oklahoma State Regents (1950): a student admitted but seated apart was denied equal education. Then came the direct challenge. In Brown v. Board of Education (1954), a unanimous Court led by Chief Justice Warren held that "in the field of public education the doctrine of 'separate but equal' has no place. Separate educational facilities are inherently unequal." A year later, Brown v. Board of Education II (1955) sent the cases back to district courts to order desegregation "with all deliberate speed."

marks.text: in the field of public education
marks.note: Brown's holding was about public schools. Later orders applied it to other public facilities.
Separation itself, not just unequal buildings, denies equal protection.

blocks.html: Plessy v. Ferguson (1896) upheld "separate but equal." The NAACP's graduate school cases (Gaines, Sweatt, McLaurin) showed separate was not equal. Brown v. Board of Education (1954), unanimous, held separate schools "inherently unequal"; Brown II (1955) ordered desegregation "with all deliberate speed."

blocks.title: After Brown
blocks.q: In 1955 a city keeps its public beaches segregated, arguing that Brown only concerned schools. What happened to arguments like this?
steps: Brown's words were limited to public education.
But in a series of short per curiam orders from 1955 to 1958, the Court applied its reasoning to public beaches, buses, golf courses and parks.
And in Cooper v. Aaron (1958) the Court held that state officials are bound by its interpretation of the Constitution.
blocks.a: The Court extended Brown to other public facilities in short orders.

blocks.title: The equal half first
blocks.q: Why did the NAACP start with law and graduate schools rather than grade schools?
steps: Under Plessy, a state had to provide equal facilities.
Many states had no Black law school at all, or a far smaller one; the inequality was plain and could be proved.
Each win made the "equal" requirement costlier and built precedents (Sweatt counted intangible features like reputation) that Brown relied on.
blocks.a: Inequality was easiest to prove there, and the wins built precedent for Brown.

blocks.html: Thinking Brown overruled Plessy everywhere at once. Brown addressed public education; later per curiam orders applied it to beaches, buses, parks and other public facilities, and desegregation itself took years of litigation. Also, Brown did not apply to federal schools in D.C.: that was Bolling, the same day.
